title: Agencies extend comment period for proposed third-party risk management guidance
text:
November 13, 2026
Agencies extend comment period for proposed third-party risk management guidance
- Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
- Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
- Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
- National Credit Union Administration
For release at 4:15 p.m. EST
The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Federal Reserve Board, the National Credit Union Administration, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency today announced that they will extend, until December 16, the comment period for proposed guidance on managing risks associated with third-party relationships. Comments on the proposal were originally due November 16.
The proposed guidance reflects the agencies' supervisory experience and lessons learned from examining financial institutions' third-party risk management practices. It is intended to help banks and credit unions tailor their risk management practices to the risks associated with individual third-party relationships. The proposed guidance takes a principles-based approach and, like all supervisory guidance, is non-binding.
When finalized, the federal bank regulatory agencies plan to rescind existing third-party risk management guidance and replace it with the finalized guidance to promote consistency and prudent innovation in the banking industry. NCUA also plans to rescind its existing third-party risk management guidance and will conduct its own reviews to update related guidance as needed.
Also today, the Federal Reserve Board separately announced that it will extend, until December 16, the comment period on a proposed third-party risk management guide specifically for Federal Reserve-supervised traditional community banks.

title: Waller, Considerations at the Intersection of Payments and Tokenized Markets
text:
November 17, 2026
Considerations at the Intersection of Payments and Tokenized Markets
Governor Christopher J. Waller
At “Navigating the Future of Banking and Payments,” The Clearing House Annual Conference 2026, New York, New York
Watch Live
Thank you for inviting me to return and speak today.1 I am delighted to be here during a transformational time in payments. Two years ago, I spoke at The Clearing House's annual conference, where I discussed the roles that the private sector and the Federal Reserve play in payments.2 I argued that the public and private sectors have distinct but complementary roles. In particular, I emphasized that the private sector, through competition, is best positioned to develop solutions that benefit businesses and consumers and to fulfill a clear market need.
The Federal Reserve can support these solutions by providing core payment and settlement infrastructure upon which the private sector can innovate, assessing potential risks to financial stability, and regularly engaging with the industry to better understand market challenges. Related to this last role, it's important to note that my remarks today are informed by rich, ongoing discussions I conduct with industry participants across a variety of forums, including a recent payments innovation roundtable I hosted at the Federal Reserve with participants from across traditional and decentralized finance, or DeFi.3
Turning to the timely themes of the conference, many of the sessions focused on the evolving payments landscape, including the state of competition, technological advancements, and readiness for the future. With this backdrop in mind, today I will discuss some considerations for tokenization in the payment system with an eye toward the future and, in particular, the intersection of this technological advancement with existing systems and markets. To be clear, in this context, my focus is on the concept that a financial instrument can be represented digitally in "token" form and transacted on a new platform or technology, such as a distributed ledger technology like blockchain.4
Although the terms "blockchain," "tokenization," and "smart contract" are widely used, to ensure we are on the same page, I want to give a simple explanation of each of these concepts. A blockchain is simply a database that can have a variety of management properties, such as who can hold a copy of the database, who can read the database, who can change the database, and how the database can be updated. The word block means data are added to the existing database in "blocks"—much like adding a new sheet of data to an existing Excel file.5
Tokenization refers to the process of altering the properties of one form of an asset so that it can be transferred and used on a different platform than its current one. For example, if you go to a casino, you cannot use physical currency at the tables or machines. But you can take your cash and buy poker chips to use on the tables. In this world, poker chips are a tokenized version of physical cash that can be used instead of cash.
Finally, a smart contract is simply a piece of code that is embedded in the database and can be triggered to execute an action at a given point of time or under a particular set of conditions. The key aspect of a smart contract is that all conditions of the code must be met simultaneously for the action to occur and be recorded on the blockchain. Smart contracts allow financial trades to be programmable, which is appealing for automating trades.
In any financial trades on a blockchain, there is an object being bought (say, a tokenized share of stock) and there is a tokenized payment instrument being used to settle the trade. For example, stablecoins are starting to be used behind the scenes to settle obligations among participants in card networks. title: Warsh, Opening Remarks
text:
November 16, 2026
Opening Remarks
At the Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference, hosted by the Federal Reserve Board and the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, San Francisco, California
Watch Live
Mary, thank you, and welcome.
I'm grateful to Mary and her colleagues for helping to arrange this gathering. This is my very first visit to a Reserve Bank as Chairman. I wouldn't call it a snap inspection, but I'm certainly impressed. Everything I see reflects high expectations and the inquiring, forward-looking spirit that we need in the Federal Reserve System.
It's good to have Fed colleagues with us from around the country. Central banking is a team sport, and I'm pleased you're here. This conference is an expression of the mission we all serve: One Fed. Fit for Purpose. Focused on the Future.
I also want to thank Marc, Chad, and Asha for leading our Productivity and Jobs Task Force. You're giving the scarcest of resources—your time and your commitment. It's a service to the Fed and to our nation, and I'm grateful.
This task force is one of five I have convened as Chairman. These groups are a way of broadening our thinking . . . of inviting robust discussions that take us further and deeper than fleeting data points or daily market moves. Our task forces are an intellectual investment to better equip us for the next policy conjuncture and beyond.
The common attributes of Asha, Marc, and Chad, the reason I asked them to lead, is not just their exceptional insight and experience. It's their battlefield bravery in the world of ideas . . . their intellect and their willingness to think hard about what might happen next. They, in turn, asked me to open the task force discussion to a wide cross section of stakeholders—and that's the purpose of this conference.
As for me, I always feel energized to be in this part of California. I arrived here way back in 1988 as a Stanford undergrad. I remember sitting in Green Library over Thanksgiving break during my freshman year, reading and wrestling with great works from a canon that I had scarcely known existed, beginning my initiation into the world of ideas. It was a special time to be in the Bay Area—neither boom nor bust, a quieter period between tech surges. And, today, just as I was then, I'm keen to listen to and learn from the great people and first-rate minds around me.
The current era may be the most transformational period in my adult lifetime, marked by the arrival of the general-purpose technology called "super intelligence." SI is an entirely new force in economic life and society. It demands our special attention.
Even a few years ago, the idea that we could have, in our pockets, instant access to genius-level intelligence on almost any subject would have seemed far fetched. Today, with the advances of SI, it's happening. The marginal cost of satisfying limitless curiosity—on questions large and small—is falling fast, perhaps even trending toward zero.
In the tradition of endogenous growth theory in economics, ideas are the ultimate resource. If living standards are to advance, conditions must be favorable to the generation of new ideas. It should be no surprise, then, that the United States is leading. Societies that bring forth the best ideas tend to prosper most. The implications for economic policy can hardly be overstated.
While an idea can be costly to discover, it's free to use. And because an idea is nonrival—that is, one person's use doesn't diminish anyone else's—its value grows with the number of people who use it. The Nobel laureate Paul Romer, among others, has shown that a doubling of ideas and other key inputs can more than double output, allowing increasing returns to scale.1

title: Does the Stock Market Stigmatize Banks that Borrow from the Fed?
text:
Banks may resist borrowing from the Federal Reserve during a panic if such borrowing is stigmatized (that is, viewed by the market as a sign of financial weakness), thus hampering the Fed’s ability to resolve the crisis. The problem may be particularly acute for publicly traded banks since their stock prices immediately reflect the market’s opinion of them. In this post, based on a recent paper, we track what happened to stock investors’ perceptions of a bank’s risk level right after it first borrowed from Fed facilities in the first month of the bank run of 2023. We find that, after a first trip to the Fed’s Discount Window (DW), investors became more sensitive to that bank’s weaknesses. In contrast, investors did not evince such concern when the bank took a first loan from a new facility, the Bank Term Funding Program (BTFP).
Two Ways to Borrow
In 2023, banks borrowing from the Fed had two places to turn: the traditional DW and the novel BTFP, announced at the start of the bank run on March 12, 2023. The DW accepts a wide range of collateral and provides short-term loans against the market value of the securities that a bank pledges. The BTFP provided loans of up to one year against the face value of high-quality securities that the Fed accepted in its open market operations—Treasuries, agency debt, and agency mortgage-backed securities.
Why Borrowing From the Fed Might Increase Risk Perceptions (or Not)
Borrowing from either facility is anonymous, with individual borrowers disclosed only after two years. Nevertheless, the problem of stigma has shadowed the Fed’s DW for decades, spiking during the 2007–08 financial crisis and resurfacing most recently around the bank run of spring 2023. If the same pattern held in 2023, a bank’s first borrowing would be bad news, and investors would grow more alert to bank risk. However, our paper shows that the announcement of the BTFP made investors less sensitized to the risks posed by the banks most likely to benefit from the BFTP. So, it’s possible that subsequent borrowing from any Fed facility would be less stigmatized.
Measuring Investor Perceptions About Bank Risk
To track investor risk perceptions, we build bank stock portfolios that isolate four balance sheet weaknesses: reliance on uninsured deposits, unrealized losses on securities, and size of cash holdings—all measured as a share of total assets—as well as the strength of banks’ capital. We then estimate a “beta” for each bank, where a higher beta means that each bank’s daily stock return moves more closely with each of those portfolios—i.e., investors become more sensitized to that particular bank risk (e.g. uninsured deposits). An earlier post describes this measure in more detail. The chart below shows that beta was statistically zero (i.e., the confidence interval straddles zero) before the bank run, implying that stock investors were relatively unconcerned about bank risk. Just before the run started (on March 7), the beta becomes positive and increases sharply – that is, investors became highly sensitized during the run.
Investor Perceptions of Bank Risk Suddenly Increased Around the 2023 Bank Run
Stock Investors’ Reaction to First BTFP or DW Borrowings
For this comparison we focus on the moment a bank first borrowed, when new information is most likely to reach the market (since borrowing tends to be persistent). Between March 8 and March 31, 2023, 34 banks in our sample made a first draw on the BTFP and 33 on the DW; among these institutions, 10 used both facilities. We compare each borrower with the 207 banks that used neither facility, looking at the seven trading days on either side of that first loan. Because banks borrowed on different dates, we employ a statistical approach used for analysis where an event occurs with staggered timing.

title: Can Workers Predict Job Finding and Job Loss?
text:
Workers’ perceptions of the labor market may differ from aggregate labor market statistics. Individuals might be overly optimistic about their chance of finding a job, or too pessimistic about the odds of losing their current position. In this post, we compare subjective beliefs of future job-finding and job-loss from the New York Fed’s Survey of Consumer Expectations (SCE) with their realized counterparts in the Current Population Survey (CPS). We then investigate how closely aggregate perceptions of job-finding and job-loss prospects align with realized rates.
Although job-finding expectations align closely with actual rates before COVID, we document a persistent pessimism following the pandemic, in which newly unemployed workers underestimate their true probability of finding a job. This divergence of expectation from reality is driven by younger individuals and those without a college education. While job separations are more difficult to compare directly, our analysis suggests that expectations exceed true job loss rates, in part due to workers underestimating how drastically layoff rates decrease with longer job tenure.
Are Job Finding Expectations Aligned with True Rates?
The SCE asks employed respondents how likely they would be to find a new job within three months if they were to lose their current job. To create a comparable measure in the CPS, we use microdata that enables us to follow the month-to-month flow of individuals between employment and nonemployment. We examine individuals who are newly unemployed in a given month—namely those who have been without a job and looking for work for four or fewer weeks—and calculate the rate at which these job-seekers become re-employed in the subsequent three months.
Job-Finding Expectations Diverged from Actual Rates After COVID
The chart above compares the predicted 3-month job finding rates collected by the SCE, which began collecting responses in 2013, with the actual rates we compute in the CPS. Expected and realized rates exhibit similar levels prior to 2020; averaged over 2014 through 2019, the SCE expected 3-month job finding rate is 55.5 percent, in line with the CPS true job finding rate of 57.2 percent over the same period. The steep drop in true three-month-ahead job finding rates at the end of 2019 highlights the unanticipated nature of COVID-19: as individuals did not predict the arrival of the pandemic, expectations only fall at its onset in March of 2020.
However, while actual job finding rates largely seem to recover to pre-COVID levels by 2021, expectations remain subdued for far longer. We document a gap between the two series in the years following 2020, in which worker expectations regarding job finding fall consistently below the realized rate. Although realized job finding rates have stayed at an average of 58.8 percent from 2022 through the present day, predicted job finding probabilities since the pandemic have fallen to 53.0 percent. This wedge suggests that workers have been persistently pessimistic about their chances of finding a job in the post-pandemic period.
Did Job-Finding Expectations Fall Uniformly After COVID?
To determine whether the post-pandemic widening of the gap between job-finding expectations and realized rates was driven by particular types of workers, we compare how the gap changes across age groups and levels of educational attainment. The chart below displays, by demographic group, the difference between expected and true job finding rates averaged across the pre- and post-COVID periods.
Younger Workers and Those Without College Degrees Became More Pessimistic Post-COVID
We find that individuals over 30 and those with at least some college education experienced only slight changes following the pandemic in the difference between their expected and true rates of job finding. title: Connecting Stock Market to Labor Market During the AI Boom
text:
The artificial intelligence boom has coincided with unusually high stock valuations, echoing earlier technology-driven booms. Four economic variables can largely account for changes in the stock market’s cyclically adjusted price-earnings ratio since 1961, including most of the run-up since 2022. The most important of these is the noncyclical rate of unemployment, which points to a connection between the stock market and the labor market. This may reflect that employers value the future benefits from hiring new workers in much the same way that investors value future cash flows from stocks.
The artificial intelligence (AI) boom shares features with other technology-driven booms throughout history. These include a “new era” narrative, surging investment in the affected sectors, and elevated values of the cyclically adjusted price-earnings (CAPE) ratio, a metric that can help judge whether the stock market is overvalued. The CAPE ratio is computed as the real, or inflation-adjusted, value of the Standard and Poor’s (S&P) 500 stock price index divided by the real earnings of the companies in the index, averaged over the most recent 10 years. An elevated CAPE ratio raises a longstanding and recurring question: Are stock prices justified by fundamentals, or are investors overreacting to a new technology?
In this Economic Letter, we examine whether fundamental macroeconomic variables can explain movements in the CAPE ratio. We consider four such variables: the neutral real rate of interest (r-star), the growth rate of potential output (g-star), the noncyclical rate of unemployment (u-star), and an index of macroeconomic uncertainty. We use a simple model to estimate how well these variables account for movements in the CAPE ratio since 1961, including the recent AI-driven run-up. The most important explanatory variable is u-star, which gauges the longer-term health of the labor market after short-term shocks have dissipated. A decline in u-star tends to coincide with a higher CAPE ratio, allowing the model to account for most of the run-up in the CAPE ratio since late 2022. Without u-star, the model implies a much lower CAPE ratio during this period. One way to explain the connection between the stock market and the labor market, as Hall (2017) describes, is that employers value the future benefits from hiring new workers in much the same way that investors value future cash flows from stocks.
The CAPE ratio and new eras
Major stock price run-ups have generally coincided with the emergence of some new era narrative centered on the introduction of a new technology (Lansing 2008).
Figure 1 shows six such run-ups in the CAPE ratio since the late 1800s. The first four reflect investor enthusiasm for railroads and electricity (early 1900s), automobiles and radio (late 1920s), semiconductors and television (1950s and 60s), and the internet (late 1990s). The fifth, peaking in late 2021, coincided with the spread of social networks, cloud computing, and electric cars. The most recent run-up can be linked to AI, starting with the release of ChatGPT in November 2022.
Figure 1
Cyclically adjusted price earnings (CAPE) ratio
The CAPE ratio and macroeconomic variables
As of the third quarter of 2026, the CAPE ratio stood at 40.5. This is higher than all but one of the five prior peaks shown in Figure 1, the exception being the 43.1 peak in the first quarter of 2000. To assess whether the current CAPE ratio signals overvaluation, we examine how much of the ratio can be explained by a model based on fundamental macroeconomic variables.
In theory, the fundamental stock price is the present value of expected future cash flows that accrue to shareholders. The discount rate used to calculate the present value combines a risk-free rate of return and a risk premium tied to uncertainty about future cash flows. title: Hyperscalers’ Cash and Investment during the AI Boom
text:
Hyperscalers’ Cash and Investment during the AI Boom
KEY TAKEAWAYS
- “Hyperscalers” — large tech firms involved in data centers and computer chips — have shifted financial priorities during the AI boom, reducing their share of cash relative to assets, while directing more spending toward investment.
- Investment activity has grown much faster among major technology companies than in the broader corporate sector.
- The mix of investment is changing: Capital spending has become the main driver of investment growth since 2024, while research and development remains elevated but has eased from its 2023 peak.
Major U.S. technology companies like Amazon.com Inc. and Microsoft Corp. have sharply increased their investments during the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. How did this affect the cash holdings and other spending of these tech companies? In new St. Louis Fed research, we document the impact on their balance sheets and a shift in investment composition: Capital spending has accelerated since 2024, while research and development (R&D) spending relative to assets has declined from its 2023 peak.Julian Kozlowski, Masataka Mori, Juan M. Sánchez and Nicholas Sullivan, “Financing Artificial Intelligence: Cash, Debt, and Corporate Investment,” Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis Review, Fourth Quarter 2026, Vol. 108, No. 13, pp. 1-20.
In a two-part blog series, we outline our research findings, which focus on 10 technology firms: Alphabet Inc., Amazon.com, Apple Inc., Broadcom Inc., Intel Corp., International Business Machines Corp., Meta Platforms Inc., Microsoft, Nvidia Corp. and Oracle Corp. We refer to this group as “hyperscalers,” using a broad definition that includes semiconductor suppliers alongside cloud and data center operators. We date the start of the AI era to 2018, following advances in deep learning and several years before ChatGPT’s release in late 2022.
This blog post examines how these companies have been allocating their resources by looking at their cash holdings, capital expenditures and R&D. The second post will examine how accelerating investments are affecting operating cash flow, borrowing and payments to shareholders.
Decline in Cash Holdings Relative to Assets
The first figure shows that hyperscalers’ cash holdings — measured by the cash-to-assets ratio — have declined substantially relative to their assets.Each group’s cash-to-assets ratio is the average, weighted by total assets. Their cash-to-assets ratio fell from approximately one-third in 2018 to 20% in late 2022 and 16% in early 2026. Other firms — all other publicly traded companies — experienced a much smaller decline, from roughly 14% in 2018 to 11% in early 2026. Consequently, the gap between the two groups narrowed from approximately 19 percentage points to 5 percentage points.
The decline among hyperscalers was already well underway before ChatGPT’s release in November 2022 and continued afterward. Note that the decline in the cash-to-assets ratio does not necessarily imply an absolute decline in the dollar value of their cash, since their asset base has also grown.
Rise in Capital and R&D Expenditures
In the years leading up to 2018, hyperscalers’ capital expenditures were approximately 4% to 5% of assets, compared with 3% to 4% among other firms, as shown in the second figure. The gap widened after 2018 as hyperscalers’ capital expenditure-to-assets ratio rose to approximately 9% by 2023. Following a temporary decline to about 7% in 2024, the ratio increased sharply, reaching nearly 13% in early 2026. Meanwhile, other firms’ ratio remained near 3%. The recent acceleration in capital spending relative to assets is therefore concentrated among hyperscalers.
Hyperscalers were more R&D-intensive throughout the sample, as shown in the third figure. Before 2018, their R&D expenditures were approximately 7% of assets, compared with roughly 4% among other firms. The gap widened after 2018, with hyperscalers’ R&D-to-assets ratio reaching about 11% i

title: The Changing Face of U.S. Corporate R&D Investment
text:
The Changing Face of U.S. Corporate R&D Investment
KEY TAKEAWAYS
- Research and development (R&D) now makes up a little more than 20% of all U.S. private nonresidential fixed investment, up from about 15% in 2012.
- The share of corporate R&D funded by companies themselves rose from just over 81% in 2011 to 88% in 2023.
- Software and biotech dominate businesses’ R&D spending, both in terms of overall investment and within many R&D-intensive industries.
- AI-related R&D is expanding rapidly, though as of 2023, it accounted for only a modest share of companies’ total R&D spending.
The shape of U.S. private nonresidential fixed investment has changed significantly over the past decade and a half. A shrinking share of companies’ spending has gone toward traditional categories like structures and equipment, while a growing share has flowed into intellectual property products — a category that includes research and development (R&D). R&D is one of the fastest-growing pieces of that pie: As the first figure below shows, R&D has risen from just under 15% of private nonresidential fixed investment in 2012 to a little more than 20% today, with a notable acceleration from 2018 to 2020.
In this blog post, we use microdata from the National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics’ Business Enterprise Research and Development (BERD) Survey — the primary source underlying the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis’ R&D investment series — to look at how businesses’ R&D spending has evolved.Because the annual BERD Survey’s format changed over time, we began our analysis with 2011, when its most recent structure was introduced. Specifically, we examine who funds it, which R&D categories are growing fastest, and which industries have driven spending.
Who Funds R&D?
Historically, the federal government, universities and nonprofits have been major funders of R&D through channels like the National Institutes of Health, the National Science Foundation and the Department of Defense. But as the next figure shows, businesses are now footing more of the bill, with their share of total domestic corporate R&D spending rising from just over 81% in 2011 to 88% in 2023. Over the same period, the share of businesses’ R&D spending that was federally funded declined, from about 11% to approximately 4%, while the share funded through other sources — all those not the company itself or the federal government — remained roughly steady at around 7% to 9%.
What Are the Main Categories of Investment? Have They Changed?
Next, we examine the main categories of R&D investment identified in the BERD Survey: software, biotech, nanotech and artificial intelligence (AI). An important detail is that these four categories are not mutually exclusive. Firms classify their own spending, and a company doing R&D on new AI chips, for instance, is free to report that spending under both “AI” and “nanotech.”
Software and biotech are the two largest categories of businesses’ R&D spending, and each has grown its share of overall investment substantially. The following figure shows that software’s share of total domestic R&D spending by businesses climbed from 29% in 2011 to a peak of roughly 43% in 2021, settling at nearly 42% in 2023. Biotech more than doubled its share over the same period, from about 9% to almost 19%, whereas businesses’ R&D spending on nanotech remained relatively consistent. The AI category is newer; BERD began collecting data on it only in 2019, when it stood at about 3% of businesses’ R&D spending. This category grew quickly, reaching 9% of R&D spending by 2023.
The final four figures look at these same categories of corporate R&D investment from the industry side. We began by identifying the 10 industries with the most total R&D spending in 2023, then determined what share of each industry’s R&D budget went to our four R&D categories (software, biotech, nanotech, AI). These 10 industries together accounted for 87.7% of all domestic R&D spending by companies i

title: Frank Elderson: Smart supervision for small banks
text:
- CONTRIBUTION
Smart supervision for small banks
Contribution by Frank Elderson, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB and Vice-Chair of the Supervisory Board of the ECB, for Börsen-Zeitung
Frankfurt am Main, 16 November 2026
Germany’s small and regional banks are trusted partners to the Mittelstand and households across the country, often drawing on deep-rooted relationships in their communities. They play an important role in financing the real economy and support jobs and investment in the regions they serve.
This reflects a broader European reality. Across Europe, a diverse banking sector – combining a range of business models, sizes and areas of expertise – helps ensure that households and businesses can access the financing they need.
As Europe searches for ways to strengthen its long-term growth and competitiveness, these banks will continue to play an important role. But they are very different from large, internationally active banking groups: their business models are often simpler, their activities more focused and their risk profiles less complex. A regulatory and supervisory framework that recognises those differences can support both resilience and competitiveness.
This is already partly the case. The EU prudential framework recognises the diversity of EU banks through the concept of proportionality: the idea that regulatory requirements and supervisory practices should reflect a bank’s size, complexity and risk profile, while maintaining high standards that protect depositors and the stability of our financial system.
This framework already covers a large share of Europe’s smaller banks. Today, around 75% of the banks supervised by national authorities in the euro area – more than 1,400 institutions – qualify as small and non-complex, and thus benefit from proportionate treatment. In Germany, that share is even higher: 81%. Among other things, these banks need only report up to 30% of the data reported by their larger counterparts. Supervisors also tailor the frequency and intensity of their oversight to the complexity and risk profile of each bank.
At the same time, experience gained from applying the framework over recent years has shown that some smaller banks still face regulatory requirements and supervisory practices that were originally designed with much larger and more complex institutions in mind. A more tailored approach would allow supervisors to focus on the risks that matter most while reducing unnecessary complexity for banks.
Over recent months, the ECB and national supervisors have examined where oversight can be simplified without compromising resilience. The result is a set of practical proposals aimed at making oversight for smaller banks more risk-focused, efficient and effective. Rather than creating a new framework, the proposals build on the one already in place for small and non-complex banks. The goal is simple: to preserve the same high standards of safety and soundness while reducing unnecessary complexity.
One important step would be to broaden the range of institutions eligible for the existing framework. To qualify today, a bank must have a balance sheet of less than €5 billion. But experience has shown that size alone does not necessarily make a bank more complex. In Germany, for example, a wave of consolidation among smaller and regional banks has created larger institutions without necessarily making their business models riskier or more complex. In fact, greater scale can help these banks benefit from lower cost-to-income ratios, become more efficient and invest in key areas like digitalisation and cybersecurity.
Amending the regulation to allow national authorities to raise the threshold to €10 billion, where warranted by the bank’s risk profile and the structure of its domestic banking sector, would therefore enable more banks to benefit from proportionate treatment.

title: Boris Vujčić: Risks and resilience in the euro area financial system
text:
- SPEECH
Risks and resilience in the euro area financial system
Keynote speech by Boris Vujčić, Vice-President of the ECB, at the Euro Finance Week
Frankfurt am Main, 16 November 2026
It is my great pleasure to open this year's Frankfurt Euro Finance Week. This event provides a timely opportunity to reflect on the state of the euro area financial system and the challenges ahead. It also comes just two days before the ECB publishes its latest Financial Stability Review (FSR). My key message today is that Europe needs more market-based finance. At the same time, however, a larger role for non-banks must go hand in hand with stronger system-wide safeguards.
While most risks identified in the FSR have been on our radar for quite some time, two stand out very prominently compared to the situation a year ago. These relate to developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and sovereign debt markets.
In our assessment a year ago, AI-related vulnerabilities were fundamentally associated with stretched valuations in global stock markets and the risk that market sentiment could shift abruptly. At present however, while the risk of market repricing, rather than abating, has further increased, AI-related risks to system-wide stability now stem from a range of additional factors – the expansion of external funding from equity to debt markets, concentration of exposures, quickening AI adoption and potential cyberattacks.
In fact, rapid advances in AI models’ cyber capabilities raise risks that have systemic implications. So too does the high concentration of third-party providers of critical services (notably of information and communications technology systems) on which euro area banks and financial intermediaries rely. An early-release FSR special feature published today explores this further.
Concerns about sovereign debt sustainability have been present throughout recent years, reflecting elevated public debt levels and persistently weak fiscal fundamentals in some euro area countries. Sovereign debt fragilities have further increased on both sides of the Atlantic, and are among the factors driving up long-term yields. The risk of global spillovers has also increased. Risks are compounded by inflation concerns, a notable rise in debt issuance by hyperscalers, growing government financing needs, a more price-sensitive investor base, heightened policy and geopolitical uncertainty, and longer-term structural challenges.
Turning to economic activity, over the past year, the euro area economy has proven remarkably resilient in the face of multiple challenges. Economic growth continued to expand in the third quarter of this year, although less dynamically than in the previous quarter.
But the ongoing war in the Middle East continues to push energy prices up, leading to high energy inflation. At the same time, trade policy uncertainty has not abated significantly. Headline inflation in the euro area increased to 4% in October, from 3.8% in September, mainly due to higher energy prices. Underlying inflation has remained broadly stable and wages are not showing a material response at this stage. Overall, recent energy price developments may push inflation higher, while weaker confidence and rising borrowing costs should partially contain this by weighing on growth.
The adverse impact of the energy shock on economic growth has been partly offset by an upbeat AI narrative. But the market correction following the US mid-term elections earlier this month, although contained, serves as a reminder to remain cautious about AI valuations.
Key risks to stability of the euro area financial system
Three developments and related sources of risk and vulnerability for euro area financial stability stand out.
